c-pl-multiplier.label: Everything is a multiplier
c-pl-multiplier.summary: A profit, a loss, a markup and a discount are all just numbers you multiply the cost by.

c-pl-quantity.label: Quantity changes: false weight and free units
c-pl-quantity.summary: The seller changes how much you get, not what you pay.

c-pl-rate.label: Rates (n for ₹x) and mixing
c-pl-rate.summary: Buying and selling rates given as 'n for ₹x', or goods mixed before selling.

c-pl-symmetry.label: Equal profit and equal loss
c-pl-symmetry.summary: When two selling prices give the same profit and loss, the cost sits exactly between them.

q-pl-chain.label: Markup, discount and profit chain
q-pl-chain.summary: Marked price above cost, one or more discounts, then profit % or cost price.

q-pl-weight.label: Dishonest dealer: false weight
q-pl-weight.summary: A weight lighter than claimed, often with a markup or a discount on top.

q-pl-free.label: Free units, donation and overall gain
q-pl-free.summary: Buy n get f free, units given away, then the overall profit or loss.

q-pl-rate.label: Rates 'n for ₹x' and mixed goods
q-pl-rate.summary: Costs and selling price given as 'n for ₹x'; mix several kinds before selling.

q-pl-equal.label: Same profit and loss at two prices
q-pl-equal.summary: Profit at one price equals loss at another; find cost, or the result at a third price.

formulas.text: SP = CP × (1 + p) for a profit p, SP = CP × (1 − l) for a loss l.   Profit % = (SP ÷ CP − 1) × 100
formulas.note: Always find the multiplier SP ÷ CP first. 1.144 means 14.4% profit; 0.93 means 7% loss.

formulas.text: MP = CP × (1 + m) and SP = MP × (1 − d), so SP = CP × (1 + m)(1 − d)
formulas.note: Chain the multipliers. Never add and subtract the percentages.

formulas.text: Net % = m − d − (m × d) ÷ 100   (markup m %, discount d %)
formulas.note: The same thing as (1 + m)(1 − d) − 1. For 30 and 12: 30 − 12 − 3.6 = 14.4.

formulas.text: Successive discounts d₁ and d₂ together = d₁ + d₂ − (d₁ × d₂) ÷ 100
formulas.note: 20% then 15%: 20 + 15 − 3 = 32%, not 35%. The order does not matter.

formulas.text: A flat discount in ₹: SP = CP × (1 + m)(1 − d) − flat.  With profit p: CP = flat ÷ [(1 + m)(1 − d) − (1 + p)]
formulas.note: Profit % = (chain % − 100 × flat ÷ CP): a bigger CP gives a bigger profit, which helps pick among options.

formulas.text: False weight: the customer pays for the true weight and receives the false weight. Profit % = (true − false) ÷ false × 100
formulas.note: Divide by the false weight (what the dealer really gave), not the true one. 25% short means false = ¾ of true, so profit = ⅓ = 33⅓%.

formulas.text: False weight with markup and discount: multiplier = (1 + m)(1 − d) × true ÷ false.  Profit % = multiplier − 1
formulas.note: 6% discount and a weight 25% short: 0.94 × 4/3 = 1.2533, i.e. 25.33%.

formulas.text: Buy n, get f free: each unit received costs the buyer price × n ÷ (n + f)
formulas.note: 3 free with every 10 means 13 units for the price of 10.

formulas.text: 'n for ₹x' means ₹x ÷ n each. To compare two rates, use the LCM of the two quantities so that both are whole numbers
formulas.note: 5 for ₹40 is ₹8 each. Selling 4 for ₹10 against buying 3 for ₹10: take 12 articles, cost ₹40, sale ₹30.

formulas.text: Goods mixed in the ratio a : b : c cost (a·c₁ + b·c₂ + c·c₃) ÷ (a + b + c) per unit
formulas.note: The cost of the mix always lies between the cheapest and the dearest component. That alone decides profit or loss in many questions.

formulas.text: Profit at SP₁ equals loss at SP₂ ⇒ CP = (SP₁ + SP₂) ÷ 2.   Profit % at SP₁ = (SP₁ − SP₂) ÷ (SP₁ + SP₂) × 100
formulas.note: Selling at the midpoint of the two prices is selling at cost: no profit, no loss.

formulas.text: Two articles sold at the same price, one at x % profit and one at x % loss ⇒ net loss of x² ÷ 100 % of the total cost
formulas.note: 20% and 20% gives a 4% loss. It is never a gain and never zero.

formulas.text: Overall profit % = (total money received − total cost) ÷ total cost × 100
formulas.note: Add up what came in and what went out first, then compare. Donated units bring nothing in; free units bring nothing in either.

q-pl-chain.cue: A marked price above cost, one or more discounts (maybe a flat ₹ off), then the profit % or the cost price is asked.
q-pl-chain.standard: Call the cost 100 (or CP). Marked price = CP × (1 + m). Selling price = marked price × (1 − d). Profit % = SP ÷ CP − 1. If the SP is given and the CP asked, divide the SP by the chain multiplier.
q-pl-chain.fast: Multiply the decimals once: 1.3 × 0.88 = 1.144, so 14.4%. For two discounts use 0.8 × 0.85 = 0.68 (32% off), never 35%. If the SP is given, CP = SP ÷ multiplier.
q-pl-chain.ultra: Net % = m − d − md ÷ 100: 30 − 12 − 3.6 = 14.4. When the SP is large and the CP is asked, round the multiplier: 1.156 ≈ 1.16, so 39,312 ÷ 1.16 ≈ 33,900, and pick the nearest option.
q-pl-chain.eliminate: (1) With a discount the net profit is always below the markup, so any option at or above the markup is out. (2) Estimate the multiplier and divide: options far from the result are out. (3) When the equation has a flat ₹ discount, profit grows with CP, so test the biggest and smallest option first.
traps: Adding and subtracting percentages (30 − 12 = 18) instead of chaining them.
Giving the discount amount as a % of cost (12% of 130 = 15.6) instead of the profit.
Adding two successive discounts (20% + 15% = 35%) instead of combining them (32%).
Taking the discount on the cost price instead of the marked price.
Dividing by the multiplier when the question wants you to multiply, and the reverse.
variations: Profit given on the selling price instead of the cost price.
Cost of x articles equals the selling price of y articles.
Discount plus overheads (transport, repairs) added to the cost before the profit.
Find the marked price for a target profit after a given discount.
Two successive discounts equal to one single discount.

q-pl-weight.cue: 'Uses a weight of 900 g for 1 kg', or 'a weight 25% less than the actual', possibly with a markup or discount as well.
q-pl-weight.standard: Say the dealer charges for 1 kg but gives less. Money received for the goods he handed over, divided by what those goods cost him, gives the multiplier. With a discount, multiply by (1 − d) first.
q-pl-weight.fast: 25% less means he hands over ¾ of what he charges for, so multiply by 4/3: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 = 125.33 → 25.33%.
q-pl-weight.ultra: Turn the shortage into a fraction (25% = ¼, so false = ¾ of true), then multiply the 'sold at' percentage by the inverse: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 by hand is 376 ÷ 3.
q-pl-weight.eliminate: When the options are only about 1% apart, estimates cannot separate them, so use the decimal tail: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 ends in .33, and only one option ends that way. Also check the sign: a short weight can only add profit, never remove it.
traps: Dividing by the true weight instead of the false weight (25% short gives 33⅓%, not 25%).
Treating the shortage as the profit itself (25% short is not 25% profit).
Subtracting the discount from the gain: 33⅓ − 6 = 27⅓ is wrong; the effects multiply.
Ignoring the markup when one is given.
variations: A weight that is x grams short per kg, with no discount (pure gain).
Dishonest dealer who also claims to sell at cost price.
False weight with a markup and a discount together.
Cheating both ways: buys with a heavier weight and sells with a lighter one.

q-pl-free.cue: 'Buy 3 get 1 free', units donated or given away, and the overall profit or loss on the whole lot.
q-pl-free.standard: Work out the cost of everything, then the money that came in: units sold × price after discount, spread over the free units (money = units handed out × price × n ÷ (n + f)). Overall % = (money in − cost) ÷ cost.
q-pl-free.ultra: Sign first. Even with no free units the receipts (1,200 × 93.5 = ₹1,12,200) are below the cost (₹1,20,000), so it is a loss. The free units can only make it worse.
q-pl-free.eliminate: (1) Sign check: if the best case already loses money, every 'profit' option is out. (2) The free units cut the receipts by 3/13 (about 23%), so the loss must be well above the no-free-units loss of 6.5%.
traps: Counting all the units as sold, including the donated ones.
Forgetting the free units (gives a 6.5% loss instead of 28.08%).
Treating '3 free with 10' as 30% off instead of 13 units for the price of 10.
Using the marked price instead of the discounted price.
variations: Buy 3 get 1 free with a further percentage discount.
Some units spoil or are given away before the sale.
A bulk discount on the whole order and free units on top.
Overall profit when only part of the stock is sold at a loss.

q-pl-rate.cue: Prices given as 'n for ₹x', or several kinds of goods mixed in a ratio and sold at one rate.
q-pl-rate.standard: Find the cost per piece of each kind (x ÷ n). Mix in the given ratio to get the cost per piece of the mix. Find the selling price per piece. Profit % = SP ÷ CP − 1.
q-pl-rate.fast: Costs ₹8, ₹7.50, ₹9 per piece; mix 2 : 2 : 3 costs (16 + 15 + 27) ÷ 7 = 58/7. Selling price 32/3. Multiply both by 21: cost 174, sale 224, so 50/174 ≈ 28.7%.
q-pl-rate.ultra: Multiply both prices by the LCM of the denominators (7 and 3 give 21) so no fraction appears: 174 and 224.
q-pl-rate.eliminate: (1) Sign check: if the selling price per piece is above every cost per piece, it is a profit, and every loss option is out. (2) The mix cost lies between the cheapest and the dearest; use it to bound the profit %.
traps: Using the simple average of the costs instead of the weighted one.
Reading 'n for ₹x' upside down (5 for ₹40 is ₹8 each, not ₹0.125).
Comparing a price for one count with a price for another count without a common unit.
variations: Same quantity bought at two rates and the whole lot sold at a third rate.
Two kinds of grain mixed in a ratio and sold at a given rate.
Buys at n for ₹x and sells at m for ₹y; find the profit %.
Find the selling rate for a target profit.

q-pl-equal.cue: 'Profit at one price equals the loss at another', or two articles sold at the same price with equal % profit and loss.
q-pl-equal.standard: Profit at SP₁ is SP₁ − CP; loss at SP₂ is CP − SP₂. Set them equal: CP = (SP₁ + SP₂) ÷ 2. Then find the result at any third price from that CP.
q-pl-equal.fast: The cost is the midpoint of the two prices: (2,400 + 2,000) ÷ 2 = 2,200.
q-pl-equal.ultra: Add and halve. If the third price is also the midpoint, the answer is 'no profit, no loss' before you calculate anything.
q-pl-equal.eliminate: Look at the third price first: if it is exactly halfway between the two given prices, only the 'no profit, no loss' option can be right.
traps: Assuming the cost equals one of the two selling prices.
Finding the profit % on the selling price instead of the cost.
Thinking that equal profit % and loss % on two articles cancel each other (they do not: it is a net loss).
variations: Same profit at one price and loss at another, then a target profit %.
Two articles at the same selling price, one at x% profit and one at x% loss.
Profit % at one price is double the loss % at another.

pyqs.text: A company made 1,500 units at a total cost of ₹1,20,000 and donated 300 units to an NGO. The rest was sold at a 15% discount on the market price of ₹110 a unit, with 3 units free for every 10 bought. If all 1,500 units were distributed, what is the overall gain or loss %?
solution: Cost per unit = 1,20,000 ÷ 1,500 = ₹80. The 300 donated units bring in nothing, so 1,200 units reach buyers.
3 free with every 10 bought: buyers get 13 units for 10 paid, so only 1,200 × 10/13 ≈ 923.08 units are paid for.
pyqs.trick: Sign first: even with no free units, 1,200 × ₹93.50 = ₹1,12,200 is below the ₹1,20,000 cost. Both 'profit' options are out in ten seconds.

a.note: Only the exact working separates this one: 25% loss would need receipts of ₹90,000, and the real receipts are about ₹86,308 (a 28.08% loss).

b.note: Sign check: the best case, with no free units at all, is 1,200 × ₹93.50 = ₹1,12,200 against a cost of ₹1,20,000. That is already a loss, so no profit option can be right.

d.note: Same sign check: receipts cannot beat the cost here, so a profit is impossible.

pyqs.text: A retailer marks a laptop 70% above its cost and gives a first discount of 20% on the marked price. In a sale a further 15% is taken off the discounted price. If the final selling price is ₹39,312, what is the approximate cost price?
solution: Chain the multipliers: 1.7 × 0.8 × 0.85 = 1.156, so SP = 1.156 × CP.
pyqs.trick: The multiplier is about 1.16, so CP ≈ 39,312 ÷ 1.16 ≈ ₹33,900. The nearest option is ₹34,000.

a.note: ₹28,000 would need a multiplier of 39,312 ÷ 28,000 = 1.40, but the chain 1.7 × 0.8 × 0.85 gives only 1.156.

c.note: ₹32,000 would need a multiplier of 1.23; the chain gives 1.156.

d.note: Added the two discounts (20% + 15% = 35%) instead of chaining them (32% off): 39,312 ÷ (1.7 × 0.65) ≈ ₹35,577, nearest to ₹35,000.

pyqs.text: A baker buys wheat flour at 5 for ₹40, rye flour at 6 for ₹45 and oats flour at 4 for ₹36. He mixes them in the ratio 2 : 2 : 3 and sells all of it at 3 for ₹32. What is his approximate profit or loss %?
solution: Cost per piece: wheat 40 ÷ 5 = ₹8, rye 45 ÷ 6 = ₹7.50, oats 36 ÷ 4 = ₹9.
Mix of 7 pieces (2 : 2 : 3): cost = 16 + 15 + 27 = ₹58, so 58/7 per piece.
pyqs.trick: The selling price per piece (₹10.67) is above every cost (₹7.50, ₹8, ₹9), so both loss options are out. Against an average cost near ₹8.3 the profit is about 29%.

a.note: Sign check: ₹10.67 per piece is above even the dearest cost of ₹9, so this cannot be a loss.

b.note: Close, but the weighted cost is 58/7 = ₹8.29 and ₹10.67 ÷ 8.29 = 1.287. A 27% profit would need a cost of ₹8.40.

d.note: Sign check: the selling price beats every cost, so this cannot be a loss.

pyqs.text: A shopkeeper sells rice at a 6% discount on the marked price but uses a weight that is 25% less than the actual weight. Find his overall profit %.
solution: A weight 25% short means he hands over ¾ of what he charges for.
He receives 0.94 of the marked price for goods that are worth 0.75 of it.
pyqs.trick: 25% less is ¾, so multiply by 4/3: 94 × 4 ÷ 3 = 125.33. Only one option has the tail .33.

a.note: 20.5% is a near miss: the exact profit is 25.33% (94 × 4 ÷ 3 = 125.33).

b.note: 22.5% is a near miss: the exact profit is 25.33% (94 × 4 ÷ 3 = 125.33).

d.note: 26.5% is a near miss: the exact profit is 25.33% (94 × 4 ÷ 3 = 125.33).

pyqs.text: The profit made on an article sold for ₹2,400 equals the loss made when it is sold for ₹2,000. What is the profit or loss % if it is sold for ₹2,200?
solution: Selling at ₹2,200 is selling at cost: no profit, no loss.
pyqs.trick: The cost is the midpoint of the two prices. ₹2,200 is that midpoint.

a.note: ₹2,200 is exactly halfway between ₹2,400 and ₹2,000, so it is the cost. Any profit or loss figure (Profit of 2.5%) cannot be right.

b.note: ₹2,200 is exactly halfway between ₹2,400 and ₹2,000, so it is the cost. Any profit or loss figure (Profit of 3.125%) cannot be right.

c.note: ₹2,200 is exactly halfway between ₹2,400 and ₹2,000, so it is the cost. Any profit or loss figure (Loss of 3.125%) cannot be right.

pyqs.text: A television is sold for ₹Q at a 25% profit. In a clearance sale the shopkeeper marks the same set at 1.4Q and allows a 15% discount on the marked price. What is his profit % in the sale?
solution: SP = Q gives a 25% profit, so CP = Q ÷ 1.25 = 0.8Q.
pyqs.trick: Cost is 0.8Q and the new price is 1.19Q. 1.19 ÷ 0.8 is just under 1.5, so the profit is just under 50%.

a.note: 45.75% would need a selling price of 0.8 × 1.4575 = 1.166Q; the real price is 1.19Q.

b.note: This is the markup percentage itself. It ignores both the 15% discount and the fact that the cost is 0.8Q, not Q.

d.note: 50% profit would need a price of 1.2Q (1.5 × 0.8Q). The discounted price is 1.19Q, a little less.

pyqs.text: A trader marks his goods 30% above the cost price and then allows a discount of 12%. What is his profit %?

b.note: Gave the discount amount instead of the profit: 12% of 130 = 15.6, as a % of cost.

c.note: 12% off a price that is 130% of cost takes off 15.6% of cost, so the profit is 30 − 15.6 = 14.4. Anything above 15 is out.

d.note: Subtracted the percentages: 30 − 12 = 18. The discount is on the marked price, which is already 30% above cost.

pyqs.text: A shopkeeper marks his products 50% above cost and allows a 20% discount on the marked price. He also gives an extra cash discount of ₹120 and still makes a 16% profit on cost. What is the cost price?
pyqs.trick: Profit % = 20 − 12,000 ÷ CP. A bigger CP gives a bigger profit, and even ₹2,400 only reaches 15%, so the answer is the biggest option.

practice.text: The marked price of an article is ₹3,840. After successive discounts of 25% and 10% it is sold at a 8% profit. Find the cost price.
practice.solution: SP = 3840 × 3/4 × 9/10 = 2592. SP is 108% of CP. CP = 2592 ÷ 27/25 = 2400. The successive discounts together are 65/2%, not 35%. That is why CP is not the sum-based value.

a.note: Took 8% off the selling price instead of dividing by 27/25.

c.note: Multiplied by (1 + p) instead of dividing.

d.note: Added the discounts: 25% + 10% = 35%.

practice.solution: SP = 2400 × 3/4 × 4/5 = 1440. SP is 120% of CP. CP = 1440 ÷ 6/5 = 1200. The successive discounts together are 40%, not 45%. That is why CP is not the sum-based value.

a.note: Multiplied by (1 + p) instead of dividing.

c.note: Added the discounts: 25% + 20% = 45%.

d.note: Took 20% off the selling price instead of dividing by 6/5.

practice.solution: Markup and discount: 13/10 × 17/20 = 1.105. False weight: × 1000/920. Multiplier = 1.2011. Profit = 20.11%. The effects multiply; they do not add.

practice.text: A dealer marks goods 40% above cost, allows a 5% discount and uses a 920 g weight for 1 kg. Find his profit %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
practice.solution: Markup and discount: 7/5 × 19/20 = 1.33. False weight: × 1000/920. Multiplier = 1.4457. Profit = 44.57%. The effects multiply; they do not add.

practice.text: A dishonest dealer buys with a 1200 g weight for 1 kg and sells at cost price using a 800 g weight for 1 kg. Find his gain %.
practice.solution: Paying for 1,000 g he receives 1200 g. Selling a 'kilo' he gives only 800 g. So the 1200 g he receives is sold as 1200/800 kilos. Multiplier = 1 × 1200/800 = 1.5. Gain = 50%.

a.note: Added the buying and selling shortages.

b.note: Counted only the cheating on the selling side.

c.note: Inverted the ratio of the two weights.

practice.text: A dishonest dealer buys with a 1100 g weight for 1 kg and sells at a 10% profit using a 900 g weight for 1 kg. Find his gain %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
practice.solution: Paying for 1,000 g he receives 1100 g. Selling a 'kilo' he gives only 900 g. So the 1100 g he receives is sold as 1100/900 kilos. Multiplier = 11/10 × 1100/900 = 1.3444. Gain = 34.44%.

b.note: Counted only the cheating on the selling side.

c.note: Inverted the ratio of the two weights.

d.note: Added the buying and selling shortages.

practice.text: A trader sells goods marked 25% above cost, a 20% discount, and the offer of buy 3, get 2 free. Find his overall profit or loss %.
practice.solution: Buyers pay for 3 and receive 5, so each unit brings 3/5 of the price. Price per unit after markup and discount = 1 × cost. Multiplier = 1 × 3/5 = 0.6. Result = -40%.

a.note: Gave the multiplier as a percentage without taking off 100.

c.note: Ignored the free units.

d.note: Took the free units as 2/3 off instead of 2 in 5.

practice.text: A trader sells goods marked 30% above cost, a 10% discount, and the offer of buy 3, get 1 free. Find his overall profit or loss %.
practice.solution: Buyers pay for 3 and receive 4, so each unit brings 3/4 of the price. Price per unit after markup and discount = 1.17 × cost. Multiplier = 1.17 × 3/4 = 0.8775. Result = -12.25%.

practice.text: A trader sells goods marked 20% above cost, a 10% discount, and the offer of buy 9, get 2 free. Find his overall profit or loss %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
practice.solution: Buyers pay for 9 and receive 11, so each unit brings 9/11 of the price. Price per unit after markup and discount = 1.08 × cost. Multiplier = 1.08 × 9/11 = 0.88364. Result = -11.64%.

practice.text: A company makes 1200 units at ₹50 each and donates 300 units. It sells the rest at a 20% discount on the market price of ₹120 a unit, with 1 units free for every 5 bought. All 1200 units are distributed. Find the overall profit or loss %.
practice.solution: Cost = 1200 × 50 = 60000. Donated units earn nothing, so 900 units reach buyers. Price after discount = 96. 1 free with every 5: buyers pay for 5 of every 6, so 750 units are paid for. Receipts = 72000. Result = 20%.

a.note: Ignored the free units.

b.note: Counted the donated units as sold as well.

d.note: Forgot the discount.

practice.text: A company makes 1500 units at ₹40 each and donates 200 units. It sells the rest at a 15% discount on the market price of ₹80 a unit, with 1 units free for every 4 bought. All 1500 units are distributed. Find the overall profit or loss %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.

practice.solution: Cost = 2000 × 50 = 100000. Donated units earn nothing, so 1700 units reach buyers. Price after discount = 88. 1 free with every 3: buyers pay for 3 of every 4, so 1275 units are paid for. Receipts = 112200. Result = 12.2%.

practice.text: Mangoes are bought at 8 for ₹45 and sold at 8 for ₹10. Find the profit or loss %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.

practice.text: Two kinds of rice costing ₹30 and ₹42 a kg are mixed in the ratio 2 : 3 and sold at ₹43 a kg. Find the profit or loss %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
practice.solution: Cost of the mix = (30×2 + 42×3) ÷ 5 = ₹37.2 a kg. The mix always costs between ₹30 and ₹42. Result = (43 − 37.2) ÷ 37.2 = 15.59%.

a.note: Used the simple average ₹36 instead of the weighted cost ₹37.2.

b.note: Mixed the ratio the wrong way round.

d.note: Gave the profit per kg as a percentage.

practice.text: Two kinds of rice costing ₹30 and ₹36 a kg are mixed in the ratio 2 : 1 and sold at ₹36 a kg. Find the profit or loss %.
practice.solution: Cost of the mix = (30×2 + 36×1) ÷ 3 = ₹32 a kg. The mix always costs between ₹30 and ₹36. Result = (36 − 32) ÷ 32 = 12.5%.

a.note: Mixed the ratio the wrong way round.

b.note: Gave the profit per kg as a percentage.

c.note: Used the simple average ₹33 instead of the weighted cost ₹32.

practice.text: A baker buys millet at 10 for ₹90, barley at 3 for ₹27, maize at 8 for ₹56, mixes them in the ratio 2 : 2 : 3 and sells all of it at 5 for ₹40. Find the profit or loss %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
practice.solution: Cost per piece: millet 9, barley 9, maize 7. Mix of 7 pieces costs 57, i.e. 8.1429 each. Selling price per piece = 8. Multiply both by 7 to clear fractions: cost 57, sale 56. Result = -1.754%.

a.note: Used the simple average of the three costs.

c.note: Used the ratio in the wrong order.

d.note: Took the dearest cost as the cost of the mix.

practice.text: A baker buys barley at 3 for ₹27, rye at 6 for ₹45, wheat at 5 for ₹40, mixes them in the ratio 2 : 2 : 3 and sells all of it at 4 for ₹25. Find the profit or loss %. Give the answer correct to two decimal places.
practice.solution: Cost per piece: barley 9, rye 7.5, wheat 8. Mix of 7 pieces costs 57, i.e. 8.1429 each. Selling price per piece = 6.25. Multiply both by 28 to clear fractions: cost 228, sale 175. Result = -23.25%.

b.note: Used the ratio in the wrong order.

c.note: Used the simple average of the three costs.

d.note: Took the dearest cost as the cost of the mix.

practice.text: The profit at a selling price of ₹1900 equals the loss at ₹1100. At what selling price will there be a 5% profit?
practice.solution: CP = (1900 + 1100) ÷ 2 = 1500. A 5% profit means SP = 1500 × 21/20. SP = ₹1575. The cost is the midpoint, so no calculation with the higher or lower price is needed. Only the cost matters.

a.note: Took 5% on the higher price.

b.note: Added 5 rupees instead of 5%.

d.note: Skipped the halving when finding the cost.

practice.text: The profit at a selling price of ₹2100 equals the loss at ₹1900. At what selling price will there be a 10% profit?
practice.solution: CP = (2100 + 1900) ÷ 2 = 2000. A 10% profit means SP = 2000 × 11/10. SP = ₹2200. The cost is the midpoint, so no calculation with the higher or lower price is needed. Only the cost matters.

a.note: Skipped the halving when finding the cost.

c.note: Took 10% on the higher price.

practice.text: Two articles are sold at ₹2400 each, one at a 50% profit and the other at a 50% loss. Find the total gain or loss in rupees.
practice.solution: Costs: 2400 ÷ 3/2 = 1600 and 2400 ÷ 1/2 = 4800. Total cost = 6400. Total selling price = 4800. The difference is a loss of 1600. As a % of total cost it is 50²/100 = 25%. It is never a gain.

a.note: Thought +50% and −50% cancel.

c.note: Got the size right but the sign wrong.

d.note: Took 50% of the total selling price.

practice.text: Two articles are sold at ₹1200 each, one at a 20% profit and the other at a 20% loss. Find the total gain or loss in rupees.
practice.solution: Costs: 1200 ÷ 6/5 = 1000 and 1200 ÷ 4/5 = 1500. Total cost = 2500. Total selling price = 2400. The difference is a loss of 100. As a % of total cost it is 20²/100 = 4%. It is never a gain.

a.note: Got the size right but the sign wrong.

b.note: Thought +20% and −20% cancel.

c.note: Took 20% of the total selling price.
